en: A certain Yakṣa, having neglected his duty through negligence caused by the heavy sorrow of separation from his beloved,
had his majesty eclipsed by a curse from his lord to be endured for one year;
he took up residence in the waters made holy by the bathing of Janaka’s daughter.
He dwelt in the hermitages of Rāmagiri among trees providing lush shade.
On that mountain, having spent several months separated from his beloved, with his forearms scarred by the slipping of golden bracelets, that lover,
on the first day of the month of Āṣāḍha, [beheld] a cloud embracing the mountain peak.
He beheld a sight as beautiful to behold as an elephant engaged in play upon a rampart.

Standing somehow before him for the sake of curiosity, the attendant of the King of Kings brooded for a long time with tears welling within; for even the mind of one who is happy undergoes a change upon seeing a cloud.
How much more so, then, when the person who longs for the embrace of one's neck is situated at a great distance?
When the monsoon had approached, he— seeking a means to sustain the life of his beloved and wishing to send news consisting of his own welfare by means of a cloud—
to that cloud, for whom he had prepared an offering of fresh *kuṭaja* flowers, [spoke].
Pleased, he uttered words of welcome, beginning with expressions of joy.
"Where is the cloud— a mere confluence of smoke, light, water, and wind—
and where are the meanings of a message, which must be delivered by living beings with functional senses?
Thinking thus, the Guhyaka, disregarding such considerations out of eagerness, made his request to him.
For those afflicted by desire are by nature wretched among both sentient and insentient beings. // 1.5 //
Born in the world-renowned lineage of the Puṣkarāvartakas, I know you to be the innate companion of Indra, able to assume any form at will;
therefore, by the power of fate, I have come to you as a suppliant, though my kin are far away.
A request made to one of superior virtue is better, even if it fails, than one made to a base person that succeeds in obtaining its desire.

O cloud, you are the refuge for those who are tormented; therefore, carry my message to my beloved, who has been separated from me by the wrath of the Lord of Wealth. Your destination is the abode named Alakā, belonging to the lords of the Yakṣas.
Her palace was washed by the moonlight from the head of Hara situated in the outer garden.
When you have ascended the path of the wind, the wives of travelers, drawing back their long tresses and breathing a sigh of relief through trust, will gaze upon you;
for who, when you are thus equipped, would neglect his wife distressed by separation?
There would be no other person like me who lives dependent on others.

And you shall surely see your brother’s wife— faithful to her one husband, intent on counting the days, and unharmed— for the bond of hope in women is generally as fragile as a flower, yet your progress shall remain unhindered.
It immediately protects the loving heart and restrains it during separation. // 1.9 //
The favorable breeze gently and slowly pushes you along,
and this sweet-voiced cātaka bird, sharing your fragrance, warbles melodiously;
surely they have formed a chain together through their long acquaintance with the moment of conception.
The cranes will attend upon you in the sky, who are so pleasing to the eye.
Having heard that thunder of yours, so pleasing to the ear, which is capable of making the earth fruitful even down to its mushrooms, the cranes, longing for Lake Mānasa,
carry with them as provisions for the journey the cuttings of lotus stalks all the way to Kailāsa.
In the sky, royal swans shall become your companions.

Take leave of this lofty mountain, your dear friend, embracing him whose slopes are marked by the footprints of the Lord of the Raghus— footprints worthy of worship by men; for whenever he comes into your company from time to time, [he brings you joy].
He released warm tears born of long separation, manifesting his affection.

First, O cloud, hear from me as I describe the path suited to your journey; thereafter you shall hear my message, a draught for the ears. You shall go there, resting your weary feet upon the mountain peaks whenever you are fatigued.
Having repeatedly consumed the very light water of the flowing streams until it was exhausted, he [remained].
"Is the wind carrying away the peak of the mountain?"—
thus watched with startled alarm by the innocent wives of the Siddhas looking upwards,
rise up from this place of lush Nicula trees and fly through the sky toward the north.
On the path of Dignāga, avoiding the arrogant grasps of his thick trunk.
Before you, from the tip of an anthill, emerges a fragment of Indra’s bow, appearing like a blending of jewel-reflections; by this,
your dark body will attain an exceeding luster.
Like the peacock feather of Viṣṇu in his cowherd guise, which vibrates with shimmering luster.
Being drunk in by the eyes of the village women— eyes moist with affection and skilled in discerning the movements of the brows that signaled, "The fruit of the harvest is coming to you"—
he ascended the Māla field, fragrant from the recent turning of the furrows.
Go a little way to the west with a swift pace, and then proceed once more toward the north.
Mount Āmrakūṭa, having quenched the forest conflagration with its showers, will properly receive you upon its peak when you are overcome by the fatigue of the journey;
for even one who is lowly does not refuse shelter out of regard for former merits.
If one turns away even when a friend has arrived, how much more so toward one who stands high above?
When you, who possess the hue of a smooth braid of hair, have ascended its peak, this mountain— its slopes concealed by wild mango trees shining with ripened fruit—
will surely attain a state worthy of being gazed upon by celestial couples.
In the center, it was dark like the breast of the earth, pale with the remaining expanse.
Having stayed for a moment in that bower enjoyed by the wives of forest-dwellers, you—
your pace quickened by the discharge of water— will cross the further path and see the Revā river broken apart at the rocky foot of the Vindhya mountains.
Like streaks of ash applied in portions upon the body of an elephant.
O cloud, when you have come before him, that mountain Sānumān will welcome you with his lofty crest of mango trees, praising you;
and you, in turn, should quench his summer heat with your downpour.
A service rendered to the great, when moistened by sincerity, bears fruit before long.
Having shed its rain, you should proceed taking up that water which has been scented by the bitter ichor of wild elephants and whose current is checked by groves of *jambū* trees; then,
O cloud, the wind will not be able to shake you, who possess such inner substance.
For everything that is empty becomes light; fullness leads to heaviness.
Having seen the *nīpa* tree, greenish-brown with half-grown filaments,
and the *kandalī* plants along the marshy banks with their first buds appearing;
and having eaten in the forests and smelled the exceedingly fragrant scent of the earth—
Those deer, shedding drops of water from their eyes, will indicate the path for you.
Beholding the cātaka birds, who are clever at catching drops of water,
and pointing out the cranes as they form into rows by counting them,
the Siddhas will honor you when the time for thunder arrives.
Trembling with emotion, they received the hurried embraces of their dear companions.
I foresee, my friend, that even though you wish to travel quickly for the sake of my beloved,
there will be a delay at every mountain fragrant with *kakubha* flowers; for there,
the peacocks, with their white-cornered eyes and tearful glances, will greet you with their cries.
Even if you are provoked, you should somehow resolve to depart quickly.
With groves of trees encircled by pale-green hedges,
their village shrines bustling with the nest-building of domestic crows,
and the edges of their rose-apple forests darkened by ripening fruit— you will find these lands when you draw near.
The Daśārṇas will become prosperous, with swans remaining here for only a few days.
Having gone to their capital city, renowned by the name Vidiśā in those directions,
you will immediately obtain the full fruit of your amorous desires;
for there you shall drink the sweet water, made pleasant by the sound of thundering near its banks.
The water of the Vetravatī river, with its moving waves, was like a face with a frown of knitted brows.
There you should dwell upon the mountain named Nīcaiḥ, for the sake of rest;
it seems to thrill with joy at your touch through its full-blown *kadamba* trees,
which emit the fragrance of the dalliances of virtuous women belonging to the city-dwellers.
He displays his unrestrained youthful vigor through his stone dwellings.
Having rested, you proceed, sprinkling with fresh droplets of water the clusters of jasmine in the garden groves growing on the banks of the forest rivers,
while the blue lotuses at the ears of those women— exhausted by the pain of removing perspiration from their cheeks— are being refreshed.
From the gift of shade, he became acquainted for a moment with the faces of the flower-gathering women.
Although the path for you who have set out toward the northern direction is circuitous,
do not be averse to the embrace of Ujjayinī’s palatial mansions;
there, by the startled glances of the city women flashing with streaks of lightning, [you shall find delight].
If you do not delight in eyes with their tremulous outer corners, you have been deceived. 1.28.
On the road, having encountered the Nirvindhyā river— which has a girdle-string of rows of birds warbling amidst the agitation of its waves—
as she flows along with charming faltering steps and reveals the appearance of whirlpools as her navel,
become one who is absorbed in her essence.
For the first expression of affection from women toward their beloveds is indeed a playful gesture.

O fortunate one, the Sindhu river, its slender waters now turned into a single braid as it passes you, reveals your state of separation by its pale luster and the withered leaves falling from the trees growing on its banks.
The method by which he may abandon this emaciation must be provided by you alone.
Having reached Avanti, where the village elders are experts in the tales of Udayana,
approach the city of Viśālā, renowned for its splendor, which was previously indicated to you—
now that the fruit of their good deeds has diminished for those celestial beings who have descended to earth.
It was as if a single radiant fragment of heaven had been carried away by the remaining merits [of the gods].
Where, at dawn, the breeze— lengthening the sharp yet sweetly impassioned warbling of the cranes, scented with the friendship of the fragrance of blooming lotuses,
and pleasant to the limbs— removes the exhaustion of women after lovemaking.
Like a lover, the wind from the Śiprā river offered flattering words of entreaty. // 1.32 //

Where one beholds for sale in the market-places necklaces of bright pearls with shimmering central gems by the millions, conch shells and mother-of-pearl, emeralds dark as young grass with sprouting rays of light, and fragments of coral.
The oceans are seen to have nothing remaining but their water.
Here the King of Vatsa carried off the beloved daughter of Pradyota;
here there was a grove of golden palm trees belonging to that very king;
and here, it is said, the elephant Nalagiri, having uprooted its tethering post out of pride, went astray.
Thus, in that place, people who recognize one another delight in their kinsmen as if they were strangers.
With your body perfumed by the incense used for grooming the hair that issues from the lattices,
and receiving the offering of dances from the palace peacocks out of affection for their kin,
you should dispel the fatigue of your journey within her mansions, which are fragrant with flowers.
Beholding Lakṣmī upon those [steps] marked by the red lac from the feet of lovely women.
Beheld with reverence by the hosts as possessing the hue of your master’s neck,
may you proceed to the holy abode of Caṇḍīśvara, the teacher of the three worlds,
where the gardens are shaken by the breezes from the Gandhavatī river, fragrant with the pollen of blue water-lilies.
By breezes scented by the bathing of young women intent on playing in the water; 1.36.
O cloud, even at another time, you should remain upon Mahākāla until the sun passes beyond the range of your vision,
performing for the wielder of the trident a praiseworthy service as the drum for his evening worship.
"You shall receive the full fruit of your non-faint thundering."
There, the courtesans— their girdles tinkling at every step,
their hands weary from waving fly-whisks whose handles are encrusted with the luster of gems—
having received from you the first drops of rain, which bring pleasure to the marks of your nails, [will find delight].
Upon you, they will cast side-glances as long as rows of bees.
Afterwards, merging into a circle within the forest of tall boughed trees while bearing a twilight radiance as red as a fresh *japā* flower,
dispel the Lord of Creatures' desire for the moist elephant-hide at the commencement of his dance.
His eyes were steady and free from agitation, while Bhavānī gazed upon him with devotion.

There, as women were traveling at night toward their lovers' dwellings along the royal highway— its light obstructed by darkness so thick it could be pierced by a needle— you showed them the path with a flash of lightning, smooth as gold upon a touchstone.
Do not be distressed by the thundering sound of the discharge of water. // 1.40 //
Having spent that night on some palace roof where pigeons sleep,
with your consort the lightning exhausted from long flashes,
you may again traverse the remainder of the journey when the sun is seen.
Indeed, the undertakings of friends who have pledged to act for one's sake never falter.
At that time, lovers must quickly leave the path of the sun to pacify the tears of their neglected wives;
for he too [the sun] seeks to steal the frost-weapon from the lotus-face of the night-lily.
But if you should turn back and obstruct his hand, he would feel great indignation toward you.
When the waters of this deep river are as clear as the mind,
even your reflection— naturally beautiful— will find entry therein;
therefore, out of steadfastness, you ought not to obstruct its lilies-white waves.
And to render futile the glances of the darting śaphara fish as they leap up.

O friend, having somehow reached the branch of the *arjuna* tree as if it were held by her hand, and having snatched away the dark garment of water that had slipped from its hips in the form of the riverbanks, your departure will take place.
Who, having tasted its flavor, would be able to abandon her with her thighs exposed? // 1.44 //
Delightful through contact with the fragrance of the earth revived by the outpouring of your grace,
and being drunk in by elephants with a sound pleasant to the openings of their trunks,
this breeze will blow gently as you desire to ascend the mountain that precedes the gods.
The cool breeze is the ripener of the udumbara fruits of the forest.
There, transforming yourself into a cloud of flowers, may you bathe Skanda— who has made his dwelling there— with showers of blossoms moistened by the waters of the celestial Ganges;
for the sake of protection against the armies of Indra, he is like the bearer of the new moon.
For that splendor of yours was indeed gathered from beyond the sun within the mouth of the fire.

May that peacock of Pāvaka protect you— he whose fallen plumage, encircled by streaks of light, Bhavānī places upon her ear out of love for her son, making it reach as far as the blue lotus petal near her eye, which has been washed clean by the radiance of Hara’s moon.
Afterwards, you should make it dance with thunderclaps heavy from seizing the mountains.
Having worshipped this god born in the forest of reeds and having traversed the path—
your way cleared by lute-bearing *siddhas* out of fear of water droplets— you should descend [from the chariot], honoring the sin arising from the slaughter of Surabhi’s daughter.
the fame of Rantideva, which had been transformed on earth into the form of a stream.
When you, the thief of the peacock’s plumage, bend down to take water from her,
the sky-dwellers will surely cast their eyes downward and behold the broad yet slender current of that river, which appears thin due to its distance.
It was like a single, massive sapphire from the center of the earth, appearing as if it were a portion of the world's merit that had been consumed.
Having crossed that river, proceed toward those women whose playful movements of creeper-like brows are well-known to you, whose dark and dappled luster shines above as their eyelashes are raised,
and who steal the beauty of bees following the scattering of jasmine flowers with their own reflections.
Making himself the object of the curious glances of the women of Daśapura.
Then, entering the land of Brahmāvarta with your shadow,
you should visit that Kuru field which betokens the great battle of the kṣatriyas—
the place where the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow [Arjuna] struck down kings with hundreds of sharp arrows.
With the falling of their torrents, they showered their faces like you do the lotuses.

O gentle one, having attained those waters of the Sarasvatī, may you— having abandoned the wine of Hālā, which possesses a most pleasing flavor and is marked by the eyes of Revatī, and having turned away from battle out of affection for your kin— now serve them.
You too shall become pure within, though black only in outward appearance.
Therefore, you should go to the daughter of Jahnu, who descended at Anukanakhala from the king of mountains; she is a flight of stairs for the sons of Sagara to ascend to heaven,
and she seems to mock with her foam the knitting of the eyebrows on Gaurī’s face.
With her wave-hands clinging to the moon, she seized the hair of Śambhu.
If, like a celestial elephant hanging from the rear half of its body in the sky to drink from it,
you should perceive the water as clear as pure crystal, then this [city] will suddenly appear by your shadow as you glide along its current.
It might be as delightful as the confluence of the Yamunā at an unexpected place.
Having reached that very mountain, the source of that river— its rocks fragrant with the musk of the deer resting upon them and its peaks white with snow—
you shall sit upon its summit, dispelling the fatigue of your journey.
Her radiant beauty may be compared to the white mud upturned by the bull of the Three-eyed God.
If, as the wind blows, a forest fire born from the friction of *sarala* tree trunks should afflict you— its flames consuming the bushy tails of yaks—
you ought to extinguish it with thousands of streams of water.
For the prosperity of the noble has as its fruit the pacification of the suffering of those who have fallen into misfortune.
Should those śarabhas, impetuous in their leaping and onset, suddenly take the path you have cleared and spring upon you there to break your own limbs,
you should scatter them by raining down a tumultuous shower of dust from your hooves.
Or who indeed would not become an object of contempt, their efforts and endeavors being fruitless? // 1.57 //
There, bowing with devotion, you should circumambulate the clearly visible footprint of the moon-crested Lord upon the rock, where offerings are perpetually presented by the Siddhas;
for upon seeing it, those whose sins have been shaken off ascend above at the dissolution of the senses.
Those who possess faith will be prepared for the attainment of the state of the stable Gaṇas.

The hollow bamboos, being filled by the winds, sound sweetly; the Kinnara women sing of the Conqueror of Tripura with impassioned voices; and if your roar were to resound like a drum within the mountain caves—%The hollow bamboos, being filled by the winds, sound sweetly; Surely the entire meaning of the Saṃgīta will be realized there by the Lord of Creatures.
Having passed those various wonders on the slopes of the Snowy Mountain,
you should follow the northern direction through that Krauñca-cleft— the gateway for swans and the path to the glory of Bhṛgupati— which is beautiful with its horizontal expanse.
His foot was dark blue, like that of Viṣṇu when he is intent upon subduing Bali.
And having gone upward, you should become a guest of Kailāsa, whose mountain ridges were uplifted by the arms of the Ten-faced one and which serves as a mirror for the celestial women;
it stands filling the sky with its peaks, white as water-lilies.
He was like the loud laughter of Tryambaka accumulated day after day.
I foresee that when you have reached its slope, appearing like smooth, crushed collyrium,
the mountain will possess a beauty worthy of being gazed upon with steady eyes— a beauty as white as the freshly severed tusk of a great elephant.
When it was placed upon his shoulder, it was like the dark garment of the wielder of the plow.
And if Gaurī, having left behind her serpent-bracelet there and being assisted by Śambhu by the hand, should wander on foot upon that pleasure-mountain,
then the flood of water within the cascade would be solidified, its body formed through the artistry of its ripples.
Act as a staircase for the ascent of the jeweled slope; be the one who goes before.
There, the celestial maidens will surely lead you to the state of a fountain-house, with water sprayed forth by the striking of their bracelets and thunderbolts; unless,
my friend, there should be no liberation for you from them when you have been seized by the heat.
While they are intent on their play, you should terrify them with roars harsh to the ear.
Taking from Lake Mānasa water that produces golden lotuses,
providing Airāvata with the pleasure of a momentary face-veil as he desires,
and shaking the sprouts of the Kalpa-trees like silken garments with his breezes;
They enjoyed that lord of mountains with various playful activities resembling the frolicking of clouds.
O you who move at will, having seen Alakā upon his lap— where the Gaṅgā flows like a slipped silken garment as if out of affection— you shall not fail to recognize it again;
for she carries your celestial chariots aloft, emitting streams of water at the proper time.
Like a passionate woman with her locks woven into a net of pearls, [the sky] possessed a mass of clouds.
The northern cloud,
shaking its lovely rain-showers like charming women, possessing a rainbow like a painted bow,
with drums struck for the sake of music, and emitting a smooth and deep sound;
There, palaces with lofty peaks that scrape the clouds, containing water within and floors made of jewels, are fully capable of rivaling you through their various distinctive features.
In her hand a play-lotus, in her hair young jasmine buds entwined, the beauty of her face brought to a pallor by the pollen of *lodhra* flowers,
with a fresh *kuravaka* in her mass of braided hair and a lovely *śirīṣa* at her ear—
And where, at the parting of their hair, the young women wear the *nīpa* flower born from your arrival.
Where the trees are ever-flowering and resonant with the humming of intoxicated bees;
where the lotus-pools have ever-present lotuses and girdles formed by rows of swans;
and where the world-peacocks have ever-shining plumage and long for the sound of the thundercloud.
The nights have perpetual moonlight, delightful as darkness has been dispelled. // 2.3 //
Where tears arise from joy and not from other causes; where there is no heat other than that born of the flower-arrowed god, which is to be remedied by union with the beloved;
and where there is no occurrence of separation other than from a lover’s quarrel.
For the lords of wealth, indeed, there is no age other than youth. // 2.4 //
In that city, the Yakṣas, accompanied by their most excellent women, resort to palace terraces made of white jewels, which are adorned with the shadows of stars as if they were flowers;
there they enjoy honey produced by the Kalpa-trees, which has sexual pleasure as its fruit.
As your deep-sounding drums were struck softly upon their skins. // 2.5 //
Served by breezes cooled by the waters of the Mandākinī,
with their heat warded off by the shade of *mandāra* trees growing along its banks,
they were there where gold-dust was to be sought, hidden beneath handfuls of sand.
There, maidens play with jewels, sought after even by the immortals.
Where, when their lovers— whose hands were restless with passion— snatched away the silk garments from the bimba-like lips of the women, loosened by the untying of the waist-knots;
where, even upon reaching the lofty jeweled lamps standing before them, [the women’s eyes] remained fixed.
For those who are deluded by shamelessness, their exertion becomes as fruitless as a handful of powder. // 2.7 //
When clouds like you are led by the wind to the upper stories of palaces,
they immediately cause damage to the paintings with their spray of water droplets; as if touched by apprehension, they then pass through the lattice windows.
Worn-out [arrows], skilled at mimicking the emission of smoke, fly forth. // 2.8 //

There, at midnight, when your obstruction has ceased and the moonbeams have become clear, the women— embraced and fanned by the arms of their beloveds— hang from webs of thread as their limbs recover from the exhaustion born of lovemaking.
The moonstones, dripping with clear drops of water, cause them to vanish.
Where, together with Kinnaras whose throats are red as they daily sing aloud the fame of the Lord of Wealth,
[the gods] dwell in the grove named Vaibhrāja, accompanied by the foremost courtesans of the celestial women.
Engaged in conversation, lovers enter the outer garden.
Where, due to the trembling of their gait, *mandāra* flowers fell from their tresses;
where golden lotuses slipped from their ears like severed sprouts;
and where strings of pearls and necklaces broke as they came loose from the slopes of their breasts.
The path of the night is indicated by the rising of the sun for women filled with desire.
In that [city], there was variegated clothing, honey skilled in instructing the eyes in amorous gestures,
the blossoming of flowers along with tender sprouts, various arrangements of ornaments,
and lac-dye suitable for application upon the lotus-feet.
The single wish-fulfilling tree alone produces everything that is an ornament for women.
There, the horses, dark as lotus leaves, rival the steeds of the sun;
the elephants, as lofty as mountains, are like you when shedding their temporal ichor;
and the foremost warriors stand in battle against the ten-faced Rāvaṇa.
The luster of their ornaments was eclipsed by the scars left by the wounds of the sword Candrahāsa.
Considering that the God who is the friend of the Lord of Wealth dwells there in person,
the God of Love generally does not carry his bow made of bees for fear [of him],
yet he remains effective against the targets of lovers by casting glances from eyes directed with a knitting of the brows.
Its commencement was accomplished solely by the amorous dalliances of four women.
There, to the north of the house of the Lord of Wealth, is our home,
visible from afar by its gateway as beautiful as the bow of the Lord of the Gods; at its edge, my son was raised by his beloved wife after she had adopted him as her own.
A young mandāra tree, bent by clusters [of flowers] reachable by the hand. // 2.15 //
And here is a pond with steps made of emerald stone,
covered with golden lotuses in full bloom upon glossy beryl stalks;
those who have made their dwelling in its waters consider Lake Mānasa to be close at hand.
Even the swans, their sorrows dispelled upon beholding you, will not occupy [your lake].
On its bank stands a pleasure-mound with a peak fashioned of exquisite sapphires, beautiful to behold with its surrounding hedge of golden plantains;
"This is dear to my wife," [I thought], O friend, with a heart full of anxiety.
Beholding you with lightning flashing at your side, I remember him alone.
Here, near the mādhavī bower enclosed by a hedge of *kuruvaka* shrubs, stand the lovely red *aśoka* with its trembling sprouts and the *kesara*;
one of them longs for the left foot of your friend, along with me.
Another longs for the wine of her face under the pretext of a pregnancy-longing.
And in its center stood a golden pillar with a crystal slab,
its base bound with gems that shone like young bamboo;
there my beloved danced, accompanied by cymbals made lovely by the tinkling of her bracelets.
Upon which your friend Nīlakaṇṭha sits at the close of day.
O virtuous one, you should recognize [the house] by these characteristics held in your heart;
and having seen the figures of Śaṅkha and Padma painted at the edge of the door,
you will surely perceive that the mansion now has a diminished luster due to my absence.
Indeed, when the sun has departed, the lotus no longer possesses its own natural splendor. // 2.20 //
Having immediately assumed the small size of a young elephant for the sake of a swift descent,
you should sit upon the lovely peak of the pleasure-mountain previously mentioned,
and there render the light of the lamp falling inside the house fainter and fainter.
Resembling the flickering of a row of fireflies, it has the appearance of a flash of lightning.
Slender, dark-complexioned, with pointed teeth and lips like ripe bimba fruit,
she is thin-waisted, her eyes like those of a startled doe, and her navel deep;
her gait is languid from the weight of her hips, and she is slightly bent by her breasts.
Whatever creation there might be therein regarding the realm of young women, that was indeed the primordial creation of the Creator.
Know her to be one of few words, my very second life—
like a solitary female cakravāka bird when I, her mate, have gone far away;
a young woman of deep longing as these heavy days pass by.
I think she has become like a lotus-pond withered by the cold, its beauty transformed.
Surely her face— its eyes swollen from intense weeping,
its lower lip discolored by the heat of sighs,
and its features only partially discernible due to hanging tresses— is resting upon her hand.
The moon bears a state of wretchedness, its beauty marred by its pursuit of you.
She will soon fall within your sight— either busy with her offerings,
or painting a likeness of me emaciated by separation as it is perceived through her imagination,
or perhaps questioning the sweet-voiced sarika bird kept in its cage.
"Do you perhaps remember your husband, O connoisseur? For you were indeed his beloved."
Or perhaps, O gentle one, having placed her lute upon her lap covered with a soiled garment,
she desires to sing a song composed of verses marked with my name;
yet, having somehow managed to tune the strings dampened by the tears from her eyes—
Even though she herself had performed it again and again, she forgot the melodic sequence (mūrcchanā).
Either counting on the ground with flowers placed at the threshold the remaining months of the period fixed for the day of separation,
or relishing the union whose commencement has been cherished in her heart;
Generally, these are the diversions of women during separation from their lovers. (2.27)
During the day, separation does not afflict her as much when she is occupied with activities;
however, I suspect that at night, when there is no diversion, your friend’s grief will be even more intense. Behold, my message is sufficient to comfort that virtuous woman at midnight.
Standing at the window of the palace, he beheld her lying upon the bed of the earth, sleepless.
Emaciated by longing, reclining on one side upon her bed of separation—
like the slender crescent of the moon remaining as a mere digit at the edge of the eastern horizon;
that night which was spent with me as if it were a single moment through our dalliances at will.
Her very self, she was passing the time with hot tears caused by the great sorrow of separation.

Her eyes, heavy with tears, were covering her lashes which were weighed down by the water; she had turned her face toward his feet— which were cool with nectar and entered the path of her hands— out of former affection, and then turned back again in the same way.
Like a land-lotus on a cloudy day, she was neither fully awake nor asleep.

She was tossing her long, coarse tresses— which had become rough from bathing in pure water— with sighs that distressed her bud-like lower lip; she was surely longing for sleep, wondering how my union with her might come to pass, even if only in a dream.
Longing [for him], her space obstructed by a flood of tears from her eyes. // 2.31 //
On the first day of our separation, she bound her hair into a single braid, casting aside her wreath;
now that the curse has ended and her grief has dissolved, she will have me untie it— she who repeatedly brushes away with her long nails the tresses soiled by my touch.
With her hand, she [untied] the single braid from the curve of her cheek, which was stiff and uneven.
Having cast off her ornaments and wearing only that delicate [garment],
she will surely release even you from your tears of fresh water, while she herself repeatedly holds her body upon the lap of her bed with the utmost sorrow.
For the most part, everyone becomes one whose conduct is compassionate and whose inner self is moist with sympathy. // 2.33 //
I know that your friend’s heart is filled with affection for me;
therefore, in this first separation, I imagine her to be as she is.
It is surely not the conceit of being fortunate that makes me so talkative.
"O brother, everything that I have told you will soon be directly perceived by you."

I suspect that as you drew near, the eye of the deer-eyed maiden— its outward gaze blocked by her curls, devoid of the luster of collyrium, and having forgotten the play of its brows due to her abstinence from wine— throbbed at the upper corner.
"By the agitation of the fish, it shall attain the beauty of a swaying blue lotus. // 2.35 //
And her left hand, being released from the marks of my fingernails and by the turn of fate compelled to abandon its long-accustomed string of pearls,
was fit for me to massage at the conclusion of our union.
Her thigh, fair as the trunk of a fresh plantain tree, will begin to tremble.
O Cloud, at that time, if she should be enjoying the comfort of sleep,
sit beside her and endure for just one watch, refraining from thunder;
let it not be that, having somehow found me, her lover, in a dream, she should be startled awake by your roar.
Immediately embracing him with a firm embrace, the knot of her vine-like arms slipped from his neck.
Having raised her up with a breeze cooled by his own spray of water,
and having revived her along with the fresh clusters of *mālatī* flowers, he—
containing lightning within— stood at the window accompanied by you, gazing at her whose eyes were fixed in stillness.
Being firm in speech, you should proceed to address the proud lady with words as resonant as thunder.
O lady who has not been widowed, know me to be the cloud, the beloved friend of your husband;
I have come into your presence with his messages stored within my heart,
I who hasten the throngs of travelers weary on the road.
With deep and melodious sounds, [the birds] were eager for the loosening of the women's braids.
When this has been told, O gentle one, she— like Sītā looking up at the son of the Wind—
will gaze upon you with a heart swelling with longing, and having honored you,
she will listen with rapt attention to what follows this, for such is the nature of women.
The news of my beloved, brought by a friend, is only slightly less than the joy of union itself.
"O long-lived one, for my sake and to do yourself a favor,
you should speak thus: 'Your companion, staying at the hermitage of Rāmagiri,
unharmed and separated from you, O frail lady, inquires after your welfare.'"
This alone is what should be spoken first to living beings who easily encounter calamities. 2.41.
With limb to limb—slender with the slender, scorched with the scorched;
with tears meeting tears, with longing unceasing with the longing;
with hot sighs meeting sighs more fervent still—the one standing far away [embraces] the other.
With those very volitions, he enters [the womb], his path blocked by the enemy that is destiny.
That which you were indeed eager to whisper into the ear of your friends before them out of a longing to touch their faces— that [whisper],
having passed beyond the range of hearing, was not seen by their eyes.
With words composed out of longing, she says this to you through my mouth.
In the dark shadows I perceive her limbs; in the glances of startled does, her downward casts of eye; in the moon, the radiance of her face; in the plumage of peacocks, her tresses;
and in the slender ripples of the river, the play of her eyebrows.
Alas, O fierce one, there is not even a single point of likeness between you and anyone else anywhere! 2.44.
Having painted you upon a stone with mineral pigments as if you were angry in love,
I wish to depict myself fallen at your feet;
yet before I can do so, my vision is repeatedly obscured by a flood of tears.
Cruel as he is, even Fate does not permit our union there.
O young girl, the five-arrowed god [Kāma] torments me, though I have grown thin and am far away from this face of yours, which is fragrant like ground sprinkled with streams of water;
consider, then, how these days might pass during this end of summer!
Where the sunlight was dispersed by dense, widespread clouds clinging to the quarters of the sky. // 2.45a //
When you had somehow been found by me in the visions of my dreams, I stretched out my arms toward the sky for the sake of a merciless embrace; surely,
many times the local deities did not fail to behold me as I did so.
Teardrops as large as pearls fall upon the tender sprouts of the trees.

O virtuous lady, those breezes from the snowy mountains, which immediately burst open the leaf-buds of the *devadāru* trees and proceed toward the south fragrant with the flow of their resinous milk— those very winds are now being embraced by me.
"If indeed your body had been touched by these before," so it was said.
"How can the three watches of the night, whose hours are so long, be shortened like a single moment?
And how might even the day have its heat become faint in every circumstance?"—
thus does my heart, O tremulous-eyed one, find its desires difficult to attain.
It has been rendered defenseless by the intensely burning agonies of separation from you.
Indeed, by reflecting much upon myself, I support myself by my own strength;
therefore, O auspicious lady, you too must not fall into excessive despondency.
For whom has absolute happiness ever arrived, or suffering in its entirety?
The life-stage moves downward and upward like the rim of a wheel. (2.49)
My curse shall end when the wielder of the Śārṅga bow rises from his serpent-couch;
until then, close your eyes and pass the remaining four months.
Afterwards, we two shall together fulfill each of those various desires of our hearts, now multiplied by the intensity of our separation.
We shall enjoy ourselves during nights filled with the full moonlight of autumn.
Furthermore, you said: "Formerly, while clinging to my neck on our bed, you fell asleep and then woke up weeping quite loudly;
when I asked you repeatedly, you spoke with a suppressed laugh."
"I saw you in a dream, O rogue, delighting some woman."
Knowing from this gift of proof that I am well,
O dark-eyed one, do not become distrustful of me because of rumors; for they say that affections are destroyed by separation, yet they are indestructible when not enjoyed.
When directed toward a beloved object, those whose essence has been accumulated become a mass of love.

Having thus consoled your friend, who was overcome with intense grief at their first separation, you quickly descended from the mountain whose peaks were uprooted by the bull of the Three-eyed God; and by those words of hers, sent along with tokens of recognition and inquiries after my welfare, you [comforted] me as well.
In the morning, you should sustain your life, as fragile as a jasmine blossom.

O gentle one, I trust you have resolved to perform this service for my kin; indeed, from your silence, I do not perceive any firm resolve in you, yet even when unbidden, you grant water to the *cātaka* birds when they beg for it.
For it has been said that for the virtuous, the very act of accomplishing the desired aim of those who seek them is their response. (2.54)
